In fiscal 2013 we opened additional showrooms in Hong Kong and the United Kingdom, and opened showrooms for the first time in Germany, Singapore, the Netherlands, and China. 
 Basis of Presentation 
 Net revenue is comprised of:

• 
 corporate-owned store net revenue, which includes sales to customers through corporate-owned stores in the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand;

• 
 other net revenue, which includes wholesale accounts, franchise sales, warehouse sales, outlets and sales from company-operated showrooms.

• 
 the cost incurred to deliver inventory to our distribution centers including freight, non-refundable taxes, duty and other landing costs;

Results of Operations 
 The following tables summarize key components of our results of operations for the periods indicated, both in dollars and as a percentage of net revenue:

Comparison of Fiscal 2013 to Fiscal 2012 
 Net Revenue 
 Net revenue increased $220.8 million , or 16% , to $1.591 billion in fiscal 2013 from $1.370 billion in fiscal 2012 . Assuming the average exchange rates in fiscal 2013 remained constant with the average exchange rates in fiscal 2012 , our net revenue would have increase d $247.0 million , or 18% . Total comparable sales, including comparable stores and direct to consumer, increased 7% in fiscal 2013, or 9% excluding the effect of foreign currency fluctuations. 
 The net revenue increase was driven by sales from new stores opened, the growth of our direct to consumer segment, and increased sales at locations in our comparable stores base. The constant dollar increase in comparable store sales was driven primarily by the strength of our existing product lines, successful introduction of new products and increasing recognition of the lululemon athletica brand name, especially at our U.S. stores, that drove higher transactions per store in the United States.
Our net revenue on a segment basis for fiscal 2013 and fiscal 2012 are expressed in dollar amounts as well as relevant percentages, presented as a percentage of total net revenue below.

Corporate-Owned Stores. Net revenue from our corporate-owned stores segment increased $138.8 million , or 13% , to $1.229 billion in fiscal 2013 from $1.090 billion in fiscal 2012 . The following contributed to the increase in net revenue from our corporate-owned stores segment:

• 
 Net revenue from corporate-owned stores we opened during fiscal 2013 , and during fiscal 2012 prior to sales from such stores becoming part of our comparable stores base, contributed $138.0 million of the increase. New store openings in fiscal 2013 included three stores in Canada, including one ivivva branded store, 36 stores in the United States, including three ivivva branded stores, two stores in Australia, and two stores in New Zealand; and

• 
 Comparable store sales increase of 2% in fiscal 2013 resulted in a $19.5 million increase to net revenue, including the effect of foreign currency fluctuations. Excluding the effect of foreign currency fluctuations, comparable store sales increased 4% , or $37.3 million , in fiscal 2013 .

• 
 a decrease in product margin of 200 basis points due to a lower sales mix of higher margin core items related to the pull-back of black Luon pants, along with higher markdowns and an increase in provision for inventories charged to cost of sales; and

The decrease in gross margin was partially offset by a decrease in expenses related to our product and supply chain departments, relative to the increase in net revenue, and by leverage on fixed costs, such as depreciation and occupancy costs, which together contributed to an increase in gross margin of 20 basis points.

• 
 an increase in variable costs such as distribution costs, credit card fees and packaging related to our direct to consumer segment of $7.3 million as a result of increased sales volume;

• 
 an increase in administrative costs related to our direct to consumer segment of $5.3 million associated with the growth in this channel and increased head count to support it;

Net Revenue

investigator.summary: Management's revenue growth drivers (new stores, direct-to-consumer, comparable sales) are corroborated by segment data. Receivables remain trivial (2-3 days sales outstanding) consistent with a retail/DTC model; the 87% increase is on a $6M base and does not contradict the growth story. Operating cash flow was flat despite higher revenue and net income, but management offers no explanation in the provided MD&A; the decline in current liabilities ($19.9M) likely absorbed cash, leaving the cash-flow pattern unverified but not inconsistent.

rebuttals.innocent_explanation: Management's stated revenue drivers (new stores, DTC growth, comparable sales) are directly corroborated by segment revenue data showing corporate-owned stores revenue increased $138.8M, with new stores contributing $138.0M and comparable store sales adding $19.5M, together accounting for the segment growth.

The 87% receivables increase represents only a $5.5M absolute rise on a $6.4M base, leaving days sales outstanding at a trivial 3 days, consistent with a retail/DTC model where most sales are cash or credit card settled quickly.

The flat operating cash flow despite higher net income is mechanically explained by a $19.9M decrease in current liabilities (a use of cash), which offset the earnings increase; this working capital shift is visible in the reported balance sheets.

The Beneish M-score flag stems solely from the DSRI component reflecting a large percentage receivables increase on an immaterial $5.5M base, which does not indicate earnings manipulation in a business with negligible receivables.
The evidence pack contains no quarterly revenue or receivables data (E25), so intra-year timing or channel loading cannot be assessed; this is a data limitation, not a negative finding.

red_team.overall: The investigator's verdict stands because the primary revenue growth drivers are quantitatively corroborated by segment data, and the flagged items (receivables, M-score, cash flow) are either immaterial in absolute terms or explained by visible working capital changes, with no evidence of manipulation.

rebuttals.innocent_explanation: Revenue growth is driven by new store openings and comparable store sales gains as reported in segment results. Corporate-owned store revenue rose $138.8M (13%), with $138.0M from 43 new stores opened in FY2013 and $19.5M from a 2% comp store increase. The remaining ~$82M of total revenue growth aligns with the 'other net revenue' segment (wholesale, franchise, showrooms, direct-to-consumer) which management identifies as a growth driver.

The receivables increase of $5.5M (87%) is negligible in absolute terms ($11.9M vs $1.59B revenue) and DSO remains at only 3 days, consistent with a cash/credit-card retail model. Flat operating cash flow despite higher net income reflects a $175.6M working capital investment: current assets rose $155.7M while current liabilities fell $19.9M, likely funding inventory for 43 new stores and international showroom expansion.

The Beneish M-score flag is a false positive caused by the tiny receivables base ($6.4M to $11.9M) generating a large percentage change (DSRI=1.61) but trivial absolute impact. Management's demand-driven growth narrative is supported by 7% comparable sales growth and 43 new store openings. No quarter-level data exists to test for shipment timing effects.

red_team.overall: The investigator's verdict stands because the reported numbers corroborate management's stated revenue drivers and the flagged signals (receivables growth, Beneish M-score) are explained by benign factors: a trivial receivables base and working capital investment for store expansion.

rulings.reason: Management attributes revenue growth to three drivers: new stores, comparable store sales, and direct-to-consumer/other net revenue growth. The pack provides segment numbers for corporate-owned stores (E34-E36), showing $138.8M growth from that segment, with $138.0M from new stores and $19.5M from comp stores. However, total revenue grew $220.8M (E1, E12), leaving ~$82M unexplained by the corporate-owned store segment. The 'other net revenue' segment (which includes DTC, wholesale, franchise, showrooms) is cited as a growth driver (E28-E29, E32), but its dollar amounts for FY2012 and FY2013 are not in the evidence pack (E33 references a table not provided). Without those reported segment numbers, the size of the third driver cannot be verified.

Receivables grew $5.5M (87%) but from a $6.4M base to $11.9M (E7, E18), keeping DSO at 2→3 days (E23), consistent with a cash/credit-card retail model. Operating cash flow was flat ($280.1M → $278.3M) despite net income rising $8.9M (E5, E6, E16, E17, E24). Current assets rose $155.7M (E8, E19) while current liabilities fell $19.9M (E11, E22), a $175.6M increase in net working capital that would absorb cash earnings. The magnitude of the working capital shift is large enough to explain the CFO pattern, and the receivables change is too small to indicate channel stuffing.

The Beneish M-score flag (E26) is driven by DSRI=1.61, which reflects receivables growing 87% vs revenue 16% (E23). However, absolute receivables are trivial ($11.9M vs $1.59B revenue, E12, E18), so the DSRI signal is a base-effect artifact, not evidence of channel stuffing. Management's demand-driven growth narrative (E32) is supported by 7% comparable sales growth and 43 new store openings (E35). No quarterly data exists to test shipment timing (E25), but the available numbers do not contradict the demand-driven explanation.

judge.deciding_evidence: Finding 0 hinges on the missing 'other net revenue' segment table (referenced in E33 but not in pack). Finding 1 is decided by the $155.7M current asset increase and $19.9M current liability decrease (E8, E11, E19, E22). Finding 2 is decided by the tiny absolute receivables ($11.9M, E18) versus revenue ($1,591.2M, E12).
evidence_that_would_settle_it: The segment revenue table for 'other net revenue' (wholesale, franchise, showrooms, direct-to-consumer) for FY2012 and FY2013 from the 10-K, which would show whether that segment grew by ~$82M and corroborate the third driver.
Quarterly revenue and receivables data for FY2013 to test for year-end shipment timing effects that could inflate receivables or revenue.

MiMedx Group, FY ending 2012-12-31. Management says: Financing cash flow decrease due to lower warrant/option exercises and Surgical Biologics acquisition payment (E30)
Numbers show: Describes financing cash flow components; does not address operating cash flow or receivables per E30
Fit in sample 1: fits. Evidence: E30.
Questions for management: What drove the 248.6% revenue growth (organic demand, acquisitions, channel loading, pricing)? Why did receivables grow 304.5% vs 248.6% revenue growth, pushing DSO from 89 to 103 days? What specific changes in credit terms, customer mix, or shipment timing explain the receivables buildup? Why did operating cash flow improve less than net income (CFO -$3.4M vs NI -$7.7M in 2012)? Were there changes in payment terms, channel stuffing, or revenue recognition timing that contributed to the revenue and receivables patterns? What were the primary drivers of the 248.6% revenue increase (e.g., volume, price, new products, acquisitions, channel loading)? Why did receivables grow 304.5% versus 248.6% revenue growth, and why did DSO increase from 89 to 103 days (e.g., longer payment terms, shipment timing, customer mix)? What specific working-capital or non-cash items drove the $3.3M improvement in operating cash flow despite continued net losses and a large receivables build? What specific demand drivers (new products, market expansion, pricing, acquisitions) caused the 248.6% revenue increase? Why did receivables grow 304.5% vs 248.6% revenue growth, pushing DSO from 89 to 103 days — was this due to longer payment terms, channel loading, shipment timing, or collection issues? What portion of the revenue growth came from the Surgical Biologics acquisition (referenced in E30 as a $427K financing outflow), and what was the acquired revenue contribution? Why did operating cash flow remain negative (-$3.4M) despite $19.3M incremental revenue? What working capital changes (receivables, inventory, payables) drove the gap? Can you provide quarterly revenue and receivables data to assess whether Q4 shipment timing or channel loading inflated year-end receivables?
